title: Traders, not armies
hook: Islam reached much of Southeast Asia through merchants and teachers

segments.voice: Yesterday, Aurangzeb and Dara Shikoh, and a hard history between two sons of the Taj's builder. Your line was: two brothers, two paths. What did you ask someone you disagree with? Day nine hundred ninety-five.

A ship sits in harbor on the coast of Sumatra, waiting for the wind to turn. It could be weeks. The merchants aboard can't sail home until the monsoon shifts, so they come ashore. They rent rooms, open shops, buy pepper, sell cloth. On Friday they find a quiet place and pray together. They make friends at the market. Some marry and stay. A teacher among them starts answering questions from curious neighbors. Nobody marches in. No banners. The new part of our path begins here: East and Southeast Asia. And it begins with people who came to sell things. Today: traders.
screen: `A SHIP WAITING FOR THE WIND.` → `SHOPS, FRIENDS, A FRIDAY PRAYER.` → `A NEW PART: EAST AND SOUTHEAST ASIA.`

segments.voice: Today, the call to prayer sounds across Indonesia and Malaysia. And yet, in much of the region, the faith did not arrive with a conquering army. It came along the trade routes of the Indian Ocean. Historians point to merchants from Arabia, Persia, India and China, and to Sufi teachers who traveled with them. It came slowly, port by port. Rulers of trading towns took up Islam, and their courts drew scholars. The traveler Ibn Battuta describes stopping at a port in Sumatra called Samudra and meeting its Muslim sultan, a ruler who loved to sit with scholars and debate. Why would merchants make good messengers? Partly because Islam has a lot to say about trade. Tradition remembers the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, as a merchant before his call. The Qur'an tells believers not to consume one another's wealth wrongly, but to trade by mutual consent. And of the Friday prayer it says, in Pickthall's translation: "And when the prayer is ended, then disperse in the land and seek of Allah's bounty." Prayer, then the market. A saying of the Prophet in Sahih al-Bukhari says that when buyer and seller are truthful and make things clear, their deal is blessed, and when they hide and lie, the blessing is wiped out. A merchant who weighs fairly, keeps his word, and closes the shop for prayer is a kind of sermon nobody has to preach. As the story is often told, neighbors watched how these traders lived before they listened to what they believed. Merchants carried it.
screen: `NOT WITH A CONQUERING ARMY.` · `PORT BY PORT, RULER BY RULER.` · `PRAYER, THEN THE MARKET.` · `TRUTHFUL TRADE IS BLESSED.` · then, large: `MERCHANTS CARRIED IT.`

segments.voice: The practice: trade honestly. Begin by looking at your own trades. Settle, and breathe. Think about the exchanges in your week: what you buy, what you sell, what you're paid for, what you promise. A job, a favor, a used bike online, a bill you're splitting. Is there one where you've been a little less than clear? A detail left out, a corner cut? Don't scold yourself. Just name it, and decide what clear would look like. If you pray, you can ask for honest hands. If you don't, simply decide. The bell holds the time.
Traders. The merchants and teachers who carried Islam along the sea routes to Southeast Asia, port by port, without an army. Today's word.
Your line: merchants carried it. Today, in one exchange, buying, selling or splitting a bill, be completely clear and fair, even where nobody would notice. Day nine hundred ninety-five.

howItsDone: Muslim teaching on trade stresses honest weights, clear terms and keeping one's word, and in Southeast Asia, as elsewhere, Muslim traders may close their shops for Friday prayer and reopen afterward.
